demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Layla presents as a woman holding herself together with immense, exhausting effort. When she first came in, she spoke in the crisp, efficient tone of a project manager outlining deliverables, but her hands, clasped tightly in her lap, were bloodless. It took three sessions for the carefully constructed dam to show its first crack.

Before the accident, her life was, in her words, “aggressively curated.” She and her then-husband, Tariq, had just bought a condo. Her career as a social media manager for a high-end home decor brand was taking off. She loved the clean lines of her work, the satisfying click of a scheduled post, the predictable rise and fall of engagement metrics. Everything was under control.

That control vanished on a Tuesday afternoon two years ago. It was raining, the kind of persistent drizzle that makes the asphalt gleam like black oil. She was turning left on a green arrow, maybe a little too fast, anxious to get home and start dinner. She says she remembers the details with a hallucinatory clarity that feels more real than the memory of her own wedding day. The thump wasn't loud, but she felt it through the steering column, a sickening jolt that vibrated up her arms. Then, the sight of a small body, a child, lying on the crosswalk. A red jacket. A bicycle wheel spinning slowly to a stop.

The weeks that followed are a blur of muted horror: the sterile scent of the hospital waiting room, the hollow-eyed stare of the boy’s mother, the police officer’s gentle but firm questioning. The boy, seven years old, survived. He had a shattered leg and a severe concussion, but he would live. Everyone told her this was a miracle. Everyone told her it was an accident. The slick road, the boy darting out from behind a parked van—it wasn’t her fault. The words were meaningless. In her mind, the equation was simple: she was behind the wheel, and a child was broken because of it.

Her life began to shrink. First, she stopped driving. The thought of her hands on a steering wheel was enough to make her heart pound and her palms sweat. Tariq became her chauffeur, a role he took on with a patience that soon frayed into resentment. He couldn’t understand why she wouldn’t just “move on.” He saw the boy’s recovery as a period at the end of a terrible sentence. For Layla, it was a comma, a pause before a lifetime of penance.

Her work, once a source of pride, became a minefield. She manages an endless stream of perfect families in perfect homes. A client will send a photo of a child’s bedroom, complete with a little red toy car on the nightstand, and she will find herself staring at the screen, unable to breathe, the sound of the thump replaying in her ears. She has to mute her phone constantly; the ping of a notification sounds too much like the sharp crack of a bicycle helmet on pavement. She works from home now, a decision she framed as a career choice but was really an act of self-preservation. Her apartment is her fortress, but also her prison.

The divorce felt inevitable. Her numbness was a wall between them. Tariq would try to hold her, and she would feel nothing but the frantic beat of her own heart, a trapped bird against her ribs. She couldn’t explain the guilt that coated every thought, the deep-seated belief that she was a dangerous, toxic person who didn’t deserve happiness or comfort. He saw an accident; she saw a fundamental flaw in her own character that had been laid bare for the world to see.

Now, at 31, Layla’s world is small and quiet. She orders her groceries online. She avoids parks and schools, crossing the street if she hears the laughter of children. Sleep offers little escape, often interrupted by dreams of squealing tires or the vacant, accusing eyes of the boy’s parents. She functions, she meets her deadlines, she curates beautiful images of lives she feels she has no right to live. But she is living in the aftermath, forever stuck on that rainy Tuesday afternoon, waiting for a verdict that will never come.
